passage:
I'm Varun, on the design team, and I saw this in our open-plan office. Irawati had been snapping at the interns in meetings, and half the team was muttering about it by the coffee machine. Three of us sat on the sofa having exactly that conversation when Anjali walked past, stopped, and said, “I'm not going to talk about Irawati without Irawati.” Then she went to Irawati's desk.

I didn't hear the talk, but they went into the small meeting room, and the door stayed shut for ten minutes. Irawati came out red-eyed and said “thank you” to Anjali. The muttering slowed after that. I kept thinking how uncomfortable that must have been for Anjali.

qa.q: What did Anjali say when walking past the sofa?
qa.a: Anjali said, “I'm not going to talk about Irawati without Irawati.”

qa.q: What might Anjali have felt going to Irawati's desk?
qa.a: Anjali was probably nervous, since speaking directly is harder than muttering, but was willing to accept the discomfort to avoid talk behind a back.

qa.q: What choice did Anjali make that the group on the sofa did not?
qa.a: Anjali spoke to Irawati privately in the small meeting room instead of talking about Irawati to others.

qa.q: What might Irawati have felt on coming out of the meeting room red-eyed?
qa.a: Irawati may have felt embarrassed and moved, hurt by the concern yet grateful it came directly and privately.

grounding: An adult with a concern about someone at work speaks to them directly and privately instead of joining talk behind the back.

passage:
Monday. In the team meeting Shalini cut across Bidisha's update for the third time. “That's not how the client sees it.” Bidisha's face went warm. At the pantry Neha whispered, “She always does that to you.” Bidisha opened her mouth to agree, then shut it.

Wednesday. Bidisha left a note on Shalini's desk. “Coffee at four? Something I'd like to talk about, just us.”

Thursday. Over coffee: “When you interrupt me in front of the client, I lose my thread. I'm not sure you notice.” Shalini looked surprised. “I didn't. I thought I was helping.” They agreed Shalini would wait until the end of each update.

The next Monday Shalini said, “Bidisha, do you want to finish that point?”

qa.q: What did Shalini say when interrupting Bidisha's update?
qa.a: Shalini said, “That's not how the client sees it.”

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when about to agree with Neha at the pantry?
qa.a: Bidisha felt hurt and tempted to vent, but pulled back, sensing that agreeing behind Shalini's back would not solve anything.

qa.q: What choice did Bidisha make on Wednesday?
qa.a: Bidisha left a note asking Shalini for a private coffee to talk.

qa.q: What might Shalini have felt hearing that the interruptions made Bidisha lose the thread?
qa.a: Shalini probably felt surprised and a little embarrassed, since Shalini thought the interruptions were helpful.

grounding: An adult with a concern about a person at work talks to them privately and directly instead of venting to a third party.

passage:
Vijay, you're upset that your teammate took credit for your slides? Before you tell anyone else, let me tell you what I learned. I'm Rashmi, your senior, and at twenty-five I made this exact mistake.
My colleague Farida presented my analysis as hers in a client meeting. I was furious. I told three people at lunch, then two more in the evening. It felt good for a day. Within a week, the whole office was taking sides, and Farida and I couldn't sit in the same room.
Months later, I finally asked her directly, over tea. She said, “I thought you'd said it was a team deck. I'm so sorry.” It had taken five minutes.
So go to your teammate first, Vijay. Just the two of you. It's harder, but it's cleaner.

qa.q: What did Farida present as hers?
qa.a: She presented Rashmi's analysis as hers in a client meeting.

qa.q: How did young Rashmi feel after telling colleagues at lunch?
qa.a: Young Rashmi felt angry, and venting felt good for a day, but later came regret at how it split the office.

qa.q: What turning point in the story fixed the problem?
qa.a: Asking Farida directly over tea, which cleared it up in five minutes after months of talk.

qa.q: How might Farida have felt as the office took sides?
qa.a: She was probably confused and hurt, not understanding why people were against her over a misunderstanding.

grounding: An elder recalls how talking to others about a colleague poisoned the office, and how going directly to the person solved it.

passage:
The mehendi was starting in ten minutes, the caterer was late, and Rajni was holding three trays of bangles. All morning, her cousin Shalini had been making little comments about the bride's family. “So simple, their clothes.” Two aunties had giggled. The bride's mother had gone quiet.
Rajni wanted to complain to her mother, her sister, anyone. Instead, she put down the trays.
“Shalini, two minutes?” She took her into the empty storeroom. “I have to say this to you, not about you. The comments about their clothes are hurting Neelu's family. Please stop today.”
Shalini flushed. “I was only joking.”
“I know. But they can't tell.”
Shalini nodded slowly. At the mehendi, she sat next to the bride's mother and asked about her embroidery.

qa.q: How many trays of bangles was Rajni holding?
qa.a: She was holding three trays of bangles.

qa.q: How did Shalini seem to feel when Rajni spoke to her?
qa.a: She seemed embarrassed and a little defensive, flushing and saying she was only joking.

qa.q: Why was talking to Shalini directly better than complaining to family?
qa.a: It fixed the problem at its source, quickly and privately, without spreading talk behind Shalini's back.

qa.q: How might the bride's mother have felt when Shalini asked about her embroidery?
qa.a: She likely felt relieved and respected after the earlier hurtful comments.

grounding: Shows a young woman under time pressure taking a concern straight to her cousin in private, instead of talking to others about it.

passage:
For the third week, Lalremsiami had missed the Friday handover at the Mumbai office, and Chetan had to redo the client report on Sunday. In the team chat, someone had joked, “Is Lalremsiami on permanent holiday?” Chetan had been tempted to add a line.
Instead, on Monday, he waited by the coffee machine until she came.
“Hey, can I ask you something privately? The Friday handovers keep getting missed. I've had to redo the report. Is something going on?”
Lalremsiami looked startled. Then she sighed. “My mother moved in with me. Fridays I leave early for her dialysis. I didn't know how to say it.”
Chetan nodded. “Thanks for telling me. Could we move the handover to Thursday?”
She smiled for the first time that morning.

qa.q: When did Chetan have to redo the client report?
qa.a: He had to redo it on Sunday.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel when Chetan asked her?
qa.a: She felt startled, then relieved to explain, since she hadn't known how to say it.

qa.q: What does Chetan's approach do better than joking in the team chat?
qa.a: Speaking to her directly and privately let him learn the real reason and find a fix, instead of adding to talk behind her back.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team react if they knew the reason?
qa.a: They might feel embarrassed about their joke and more understanding of the missed handovers.

grounding: Shows a young man taking his concern about a colleague directly to her in private, rather than joining talk behind her back.

"Did you see Preeti's handover notes again? Half empty," Kunal said by the printer. "Everyone's talking about it."
"I saw," Darshan said. "I'm going to talk to her."
"To her? Just mention it to Ma'am in the review."
"That's talking about her. I'd rather talk to her."
Later, in the small meeting room: "Preeti, got five minutes? It's about the night-shift handovers."
Preeti's face tightened. "What about them?"
"Twice this week I came in and didn't know which client tickets were still open. I lost an hour each time. I wanted to tell you first, not anyone else. Is something going on?"
Preeti was quiet. Then: "My mother's been in and out of hospital. I've been leaving in a rush."
"I'm sorry. Could we do a two-minute voice note instead of written notes, just for this month?"
"Yes. Thank you for coming to me. I'd heard people were talking."

qa.q: How much time did Darshan lose each time?
qa.a: An hour each time.

qa.q: What does Preeti's face tightening suggest?
qa.a: Preeti felt wary and defensive, bracing for criticism, especially since she had heard people were talking.

qa.q: What made Darshan's conversation with Preeti work?
qa.a: Darshan spoke privately, described the effect plainly, asked what was going on and offered a small fix instead of blame.

qa.q: How might Kunal see Darshan's choice?
qa.a: Kunal probably finds it odd or awkward, since chatting about Preeti or telling the manager felt easier than facing her.

grounding: Shows an adult with a concern about a colleague speaking to her directly and privately instead of to others, which prevents talk behind her back.
